items.mnemonic: A cross on the left and a knotted rope on the right: tie the knot.
items.culture_note: な comes from a cursive form of the kanji 奈. The same kanji starts the name of Nara (奈良), Japan's capital in the 8th century.

items.mnemonic: A needle standing up, with two short threads beside it.
items.culture_note: に comes from a cursive form of the kanji 仁.

items.explanation: ぬ is 'nu', like 'noo' but short. Do not confuse it with め: ぬ ends in a small loop, め does not.
items.mnemonic: A tangle of noodles with a chopstick through it; the loop at the end is a noodle curling up.
items.culture_note: ぬ comes from a cursive form of the kanji 奴.

items.explanation: ね is 'ne', like the 'ne' in 'net'. It looks like れ and わ; ね is the one whose tail curls into a loop.
items.mnemonic: A cat sitting down with its tail curled into a loop, and ねこ (neko) means cat.
items.culture_note: ね comes from a cursive form of the kanji 祢. The maneki-neko, a cat figure with a raised paw, is displayed in many Japanese shops and restaurants to beckon in customers and good luck.

items.explanation: の is 'no', like 'no' but pure. It is also one of the most common words in Japanese: a particle that links nouns, like 's' or 'of', as in わたしの (watashi no, 'my').
items.mnemonic: A single swirl, like the circle-and-slash of a 'no entry' sign drawn in one stroke.
items.culture_note: の comes from a cursive form of the kanji 乃.
